Weights for averaging failure-rate models

Source: R/average-tdt-ttl.R
hazard_weights.Rd

Weights several models fitted to the same data by how well each predicts data it was not fitted to, from their cross-validation results. The models can be any set: any failure-rate functions with any baselines. Which models are averaged is chosen by which results are given.

Usage

hazard_weights(cv, method = c("stacking", "pseudobma"), min_weight = 1)

Arguments

cv

A named list of cross-validation results, one per model, from loo_hazard() or kfold_hazard(). All must have the same unit and the same units left out. The names identify the models.

method

A character string, "stacking" (the default) or "pseudobma".

min_weight

A single number above 0 and at most 1, the cumulative weight the models kept must reach. The default, 1, keeps every model.

Value

A tibble with one row per model, highest weight first: model; elpd, its summed log predictive density; weight_all, its weight among all the models, and cumulative, the running total; kept, whether it is kept; and weight, its weight among the models kept, which is the weight to average with (0 for a model not kept). The unit, the number of units and the method are attached as attributes.

Details

With method = "stacking" the weights are those of the combination of models that predicts best. It is the method Yao et al. (2018) recommend, and the default here. Stacking can give a model a weight of zero. This happens when two models make nearly the same predictions: including both adds nothing to the combination, so one takes the weight and the other gets none, even though it would predict almost as well on its own. With method = "pseudobma" each model is weighted by its own predictive density, allowing for its uncertainty over the units by the Bayesian bootstrap; these weights are smoother, and steadier when the units are few. The Bayesian bootstrap is random: call set.seed() first for the same weights again.

With min_weight below 1, only the highest-weighted models are kept, as many as it takes for their weights to add up to at least min_weight, and the weights of those kept are then computed again among themselves. Recomputing matters for stacking, whose weights are found jointly for a set of models and are not simply rescaled when a model leaves the set.

The weights rest on one value per unit left out, so they are less certain the fewer units there are, as when the unit is one of a handful of trials. A message says how many units there were.

Results from loo_hazard() and kfold_hazard() can be mixed, as when the leave-one-out approximation is unreliable for one model and that model alone is cross-validated by refitting. The two agree in what they estimate when each fold leaves out a single unit. With fewer folds than units, each refit sees less of the data than a leave-one-out fit does, so its predictions score slightly lower and its model is at a small disadvantage. A message names the models this applies to.

References

Yao, Y., Vehtari, A., Simpson, D. and Gelman, A. (2018). Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions. Bayesian Analysis 13, 917-1007.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
fits <- list("exp" = fit_exp, "zeroexp" = fit_zeroexp)
cv   <- lapply(fits, loo_hazard)
hazard_weights(cv)
hazard_weights(cv, min_weight = 0.95)
} # }
